name: Bilal Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Bilal. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government, and nothing you say gets your name on it. Could you start by telling me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm a motor claims handler at the regional claims centre of one of the big national insurers, second floor of an office block by the ring road. I start at eight, open my queue, and work through car accident claims: checking the policy covers it, chasing repair estimates, ordering hire cars, writing to the other driver's insurer. Six years in now, so I know the system blind.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the phone calls where someone's shaken after a crash and I can actually sort it for them by lunchtime. What wears me out is the targets: forty files touched a day, and a new screen every year that's meant to make it faster and never does. I'm on the union's workplace committee, so I also hear everyone else's complaints at break.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly that sounds like most of the last three years. Every rollout comes with a big speech and then we're still doing the same claims.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say on the union group chat that we called it, that the hype was mostly a way to scare people into accepting worse targets. I'd probably post it too, something a bit smug. And I'd remind people the speed-up pressure doesn't go away just because the robots didn't come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I keep a decent job I'm good at, with better pay than most clerks round here. The bit that touches me is the routine stuff they do automate, like the first-notice forms, because that's an hour of my day that gets swapped for more targets. At my insurer, every minute a computer saves me gets handed straight back to me as another claim to chase.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am, keep paying into my savings, and stay on the committee so we can fight the targets that come with any new tool. I'd also push for the union to get it in writing that time saved isn't just turned into extra files. I'm not learning any AI stuff, I don't need to in this world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly relief, with a bit of irritation. I'd feel safe, but I'd still be the one telling a new starter not to panic about their numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the time saved gets handed back as more claims. Can you give me a real example?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last spring they brought in a tool that reads the photos people send of the dent. My daily target went from thirty-five files to forty the next month. Nobody asked us, it was just on the board on a Monday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your savings are strong. Does that change how you feel here at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does, yeah. I've got about nine months put away and half a flat my granddad left me and my sister, so I'm not lying awake. But I've seen what targets do to people with no cushion, and that's why I stay on the committee.

say: I'd say the AI hype was mostly a **scare story** to sell worse targets.
I'd remind colleagues the **speed-up pressure** stays even without big change.
think: I keep a **well-paid job** I know inside out.
Every minute **automation saves** me gets turned into another claim on my queue.
do: Keep handling **motor claims** and keep paying into savings as normal.
Push the **union committee** to get written limits on targets tied to new tools.
feel: Mostly **relief**, with some **irritation** about the targets that never go away.
S0.quote: At my insurer, every minute a computer saves me gets handed straight back to me as another claim to chase.
fieldNote: Bilal's **secure finances** keep him steady, but daily targets already rub against him.
His worry is **work intensity**, not job loss, in this picture.
Union role shapes everything: he frames tools as a **bargaining issue** first.

steps.text: Keep working the motor claims queue and paying into savings
Ask the union committee for written limits on targets after new tools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. That one's closer to home, because nearly everything on that list is my day: checking, writing, booking hire cars, answering customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need a proper agreement before anything rolls out, with no compulsory redundancies and retraining paid for by the company. Online I'd say this is exactly why unions exist. I'd be loud about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the claims centre shrinks by a third within a few years and I'm not sure I'm in the two-thirds that stay. I'm average, I don't use these tools, and the managers know I won't. A claims centre that needs fewer people will keep the ones who smile at the new software, and I don't smile at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd get the union to bargain for a redeployment deal and a no-cuts period. I'd top my savings up to a full year, and I'd start looking at what else I could do, maybe the ambulance service control room, where my cousin works. I'd still refuse to do some online AI course just to look keen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not helpless. I've got money and a union, which is more than most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Denise, who sits next to me, is fifty-four and on her own. She's been there twenty years and has no other plan. I'd worry about her more than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd refuse an AI course to look keen, but you also think the keen ones stay. Which way would you go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, I see it. I'd probably do the course if the union got it on paid time, but I wouldn't chase it on my own evenings. That's the honest answer.

say: I'd demand a **written agreement** before any rollout, with no compulsory redundancies.
I'd say online this shows exactly why workers need **strong unions**.
think: I expect the claims centre to **shrink by a third** within a few years.
My refusal to use **new tools** makes me an easy name on a cut list.
do: Bargain through the union for a **redeployment deal** and a no-cuts period.
Top up savings to a **full year** of expenses.
Look into the **ambulance control room**, where my cousin already works.
feel: **Anxious** about being picked for cuts, but steadied by **money and union**.
S1.quote: A claims centre that needs fewer people will keep the ones who smile at the new software, and I don't smile at it.
fieldNote: Bilal admits his **dislike of new tools** could cost him his place.
He softens only if training comes on **paid time** through the union.
Thinks of older colleague **Denise** before himself, which fits his union role.

steps.text: Bargain through the union for a redeployment deal and no-cuts period
Top up savings to cover a full year of expenses
Ask a cousin about jobs in the ambulance control room

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's basically my next pay review, and then everything I do at a desk can be done better by a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments have to step in now: a pause on mass layoffs, a tax on the companies doing it, and money for people pushed out. I'd be at any demonstration the union organised. I'd say it plainly, this isn't progress if it throws millions out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think my job is gone by 2028, full stop. Motor claims is all reading, checking and writing, and a machine that does that better and cheaper doesn't need me. My whole job is reading forms and writing letters, so a machine that thinks like a person finishes me in the first wave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop treating my savings as a cushion and start treating them as a runway. Within months I'd look at hands-on work that gets the extra three years, like training as a paramedic, because the robots come later. And I'd keep pushing the union for redundancy terms while there's still a company to bargain with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, if I'm honest. Not for food on the table, but for who I am without the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner the night you first believed it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Hana, she's a nurse, that we're fine for a year but I'll need to start over. She'd probably say her ward's still going to need people, and she'd be right for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the robots come three years later. Does that extra time feel like much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's something, but it's not a life plan. Three years buys me a training course, not a career, and every other clerk in the city would be applying for the same course.

say: I'd call for a **pause on layoffs** and a tax on firms replacing staff.
I'd join any **union demonstration** against mass job losses.
think: I expect my **claims job gone** by 2028.
Desk work is the **first wave**, and my whole day is desk work.
do: Treat my savings as a **runway** for retraining, not a cushion.
Apply for **paramedic training**, because hands-on work lasts about three years longer.
Push the union for **redundancy terms** while the employer still exists.
feel: **Scared** about losing the work that gives me my **identity**, not about money.
S2.quote: My whole job is reading forms and writing letters, so a machine that thinks like a person finishes me in the first wave.
fieldNote: Bilal's money is fine short term; the fear is **identity**, not bills.
He sees the robot delay as **three years**, too short for a career.
His politics move fast from bargaining to calling for **government action**.

steps.text: Join union protests calling for a pause on AI layoffs
Apply for a paramedic training place within the first year
Press the union for strong redundancy terms before cuts begin

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is still quick, but at least you'd see it coming down the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a window and we'd be mad to waste it. At work I'd push for the union to start negotiating transition deals now, not when the letters go out. Online, same message, louder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I've got three or four years of claims work before it really bites. That's enough time to do something, which makes it worse in a way, because I'd have no excuse. With five years' warning, nobody gets to say they didn't know, including me, and that scares me more than the news itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start an evening course in the first year, probably emergency care, and keep my day job while I can. I'd save hard, maybe put the flat I share with my sister on the market so I've got cash. And I'd stay on the committee to get a training fund out of management.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy most days and properly worried on bad ones. The time helps, but it's still an end date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets sold or cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My half of the flat, if my sister agrees. And the holiday Hana and I booked for Portugal next summer, I'd cancel that and keep the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you never use AI tools. Would five years change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a bit, just so I know what's coming at me. But I'm not going to retrain into something the machine will do in 2031 anyway.

say: I'd say five years is a **window** we can't afford to waste.
I'd push for **transition deals** to be negotiated now, not at layoff time.
think: I have **three or four years** of claims work before it bites.
The warning takes away my **excuse**, which frightens me more than the news.
do: Start an **evening course** in emergency care in the first year.
Sell my half of the **shared flat** if my sister agrees.
Press management through the union for a **training fund**.
feel: **Uneasy** day to day, and **worried** on bad days about the end date.
S3.quote: With five years' warning, nobody gets to say they didn't know, including me, and that scares me more than the news itself.
fieldNote: Bilal sees warning time as a **burden of choice**, which is unusual and revealing.
He would sell an **inherited flat** share to fund the switch.
Still refuses AI tools as a career path, seeing them as **short-lived**.

steps.text: Start an evening course in emergency care next year
Sell his half of the inherited flat to raise cash
Press management through the union for a staff training fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's me at thirty-seven. That's a different conversation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to set the rules: shorter working weeks, retraining paid by the companies who gain, and proper public support. I'd say it at work and I'd put it on the union page. Ten years is enough to win a fight like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I've got most of a decade in claims, and I can leave on my own terms. It still ends, but I'd be a different person by then. Ten years is long enough to train for a job with my hands and still pay off a mortgage before the robots show up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the claims job for a few years and start the paramedic route around year three or four, part-time. Hana and I would probably buy a place now while my pay's good. I'd stay on the committee and push for the company to fund the courses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but okay. It feels like a slow problem I can actually get ahead of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of your job would you miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The calls where somebody's car is a write-off and they're crying because they need it for the school run. I'd miss being the person who fixes that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you vote differently in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd vote for whoever promised to tax the gains and pay for retraining. I already vote that way, but I'd go to the meetings too.

say: I'd call for **shorter weeks** and retraining paid by the firms that gain.
I'd say ten years is enough to **win the fight** for fair rules.
think: I have most of a **decade** left in claims and can leave on my terms.
Hands-on work buys me time to train and still **pay a mortgage**.
do: Keep the claims job for **a few years** before switching.
Start the **paramedic route** part-time around year three or four.
Buy a home with Hana now while my **pay is good**.
feel: **Uneasy** but okay, like a **slow problem** I can get ahead of.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough to train for a job with my hands and still pay off a mortgage before the robots show up.
fieldNote: The longer runway turns Bilal from fearful to **planful**.
He still frames the answer through **collective bargaining** and taxes.
Would miss the **human calls** most, not the paperwork.

steps.text: Keep the motor claims job for the next few years
Start part-time paramedic training around year three or four
Buy a flat with his partner while his pay is strong
Go to local meetings for candidates promising retraining funds

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028. What would help is a guaranteed retraining place and wages while I train, paid for by the firms making the savings. I don't want a handout, I want the company that replaces me to pay for my next trade.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who decides. Nobody on my floor gets a say in which tools come in, and that's the bit I'd change first.

headlineQuote: I don't want a handout, I want the company that replaces me to pay for my next trade.
portrait: Bilal is a **27-year-old** motor claims handler at a national insurer's regional centre.
He sits on the **union committee** and sees every new tool as a fight over targets.
He has **nine months saved** and a share of an inherited flat.
He never uses **AI tools** and admits that could mark him for cuts.
His plans shift from bargaining to **paramedic training** as the scenarios speed up.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his desk job would go before he could retrain.
whatWouldHelp: A guaranteed **retraining place** with wages, paid for by the firms making savings.
